families.axis_name: From formal self-mastery to wounded, then compassionate relational openness
families.decision_variable: When emotionally threatened, does he move to regulate the relationship through formal control and procedure, or does he move to meet the other person with direct mercy and care?

phase_contrasts.contrast: He shifts from routinely keeping distance through polished formal control to trying to use that same control under emotional threat, but now in a strained, reactive, and unstable way.
He shifts from shaken, defensive attempts to manage the crisis to deliberate procedural action that organizes punishment, separation, and custody through formal means.
He shifts from handling injury by rules, legal steps, and indirect control to responding in person with forgiveness, pity, tenderness, and care.
He shifts from active direct mercy and caretaking back toward restrained, mediated, duty-bound functioning, preserving some softened feeling but no longer acting through reciprocal personal openness.

axis_re_expression.abstract_axis: How a person balances self-regulating control with empathic relational openness under emotional threat.
abstract_phases: Habitual role-based self-control and emotional distance
Threatened control becoming reactive defensiveness
Injury converted into procedural and punitive control
Compassionate softening and receptive care
Restrained duty with fragile, mediated attachment

0.rationale: In chapters 30-41, Karenin is already an established husband, father, and high-ranking bureaucrat, so his polished formal mastery and domestic-public routine clearly place him in mature adulthood.

1.rationale: In chapters 42-63, the crisis centers on marital jealousy, humiliation, and attempted household control, which are adult concerns unfolding within his existing role as a senior official and spouse.

2.rationale: In chapters 82-109, his turn to legal consultation, separation procedure, and custody strategy reflects the responsibilities and institutional power of an adult man in midlife rather than any earlier stage.

3.rationale: In chapters 118-149, his forgiveness of Anna, care for the baby, and reliance on religious consolation all occur within his ongoing roles as husband, father, and public man, marking continued adulthood with emotional change rather than a new life stage.

4.rationale: In chapters 145-224, although described as 'late-life resignation,' he remains active in paternal and public duties, and his grief after Anna's death fits a late-midlife adult phase rather than true older adulthood.

probes.scenario: At Princess Betsy’s gathering, Karenin enters to find Anna seated apart with Vronsky while the rest of the room notices their isolation and waits to see what he will do. The company is watching, and the moment risks public embarrassment before he has spoken.
probes.question: How does Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin carry himself when he comes upon Anna and Vronsky set apart under everyone’s eyes?

phase_responses.gt_action: He greets the hostess, sits for tea, banters about the salon, then turns to a serious public discussion and never looks toward Anna and Vronsky.
phase_responses.gt_speech: “Your Rambouillet is in full conclave,” he said, looking round at all the party; “the graces and the muses.”
phase_responses.gt_thought: He treats the scene as something best mastered by form. If he keeps to society's proper surface and gives his mind to public talk, nothing indecorous need be acknowledged.

voice.note: This fits Karenin’s early polished self-command exactly: the salon wit, deliberate public composure, and inward reliance on propriety to suppress acknowledgment are all true to chapter-41 Karenin and contain no anachronism or knowledge leak.

phase_fit.note: The response shows polished, socially controlled emotional distancing—mastering threat through etiquette, banter, and refusal to acknowledge the intimacy—without the reactive strain of crisis or the punitive procedural turn of later phases.

phase_responses.gt_action: He joins the hostess and speaks on the public topic before him, holding himself stiffly and keeping his eyes from Anna and Vronsky.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let us keep to the question itself; the decree has been much misunderstood.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels the sting of the room's attention and uses discussion as a shield. If he turns his head, he fears he will betray jealousy or lose command of himself.

voice.note: This fits Karenin in his crisis-of-control phase: the stiff public composure, bureaucratic turn to an impersonal topic, and inward fear of exposing jealousy are all apt to chapter 52 and contain no anachronism or knowledge beyond the moment.

phase_fit.note: The key cue is that he uses formal public discussion as a defensive shield against felt jealousy and feared loss of self-command, which matches strained, reactive control under emotional threat rather than calm habitual distance or fully procedural punishment.

phase_responses.gt_action: He seats himself with studied correctness and pointedly leaves Anna and Vronsky to stand as a fact observed but not contested there.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I am always glad to find society occupied with something definite.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He treats the scene less as a personal wound to be mastered than as confirming evidence of a position already forming against her. To make a scene would spend authority uselessly; better to let the impropriety fix itself in full view and reserve action for the proper channels.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's phase-2 habit of converting humiliation into cold, procedural advantage: the action is controlled, the speech dry and socially edged, and the thought plausibly channels personal injury into evidence, appearances, and later formal action without any knowledge beyond chapter 95.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames the humiliation as evidence to be banked for later action through 'proper channels,' which is characteristic of punitive procedural control rather than mere polished distance or reactive strain.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He places himself with the hostess and sustains a correct, impersonal conversation, marking Anna and Vronsky only by refusing to recognize their apartness in public.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: One must distinguish private caprice from what is due to order.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: He sees the impropriety clearly, but public notice would only lower him and weaken his position. Better to record the offense inwardly and preserve the forms that will later justify him.

voice.note: This fits Karenin in phase 2: the action and thought are formal, punitive, and self-justifying, with period-appropriate diction and no knowledge beyond chapter 95, though the phrasing is slightly compressed and schematic.

phase_fit.note: The response shows polished public self-command and emotional distance—he preserves appearances through etiquette and inwardly withholds reaction, rather than acting from reactive jealousy or formal punitive procedure already set in motion.

phase_responses.gt_action: He greets the hostess and takes his place with the company, giving Anna and Vronsky no public sign.
phase_responses.gt_speech: How pleasant it is to find such good company.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The sight wounds him, but he is less intent on asserting his rights than on preventing a scene. He feels the humiliation and bears it inwardly, choosing restraint over open judgment.

voice.note: This fits Karenin’s earlier formal self-command at Betsy’s salon, but at phase 3/ch.133 it is temporally and psychologically off: the scene belongs to his pre-confession public restraint, not his later softened, explicitly compassionate and religiously receptive mode.

phase_fit.note: The response shows public composure under acute humiliation, but the thought reveals inward wounding and defensive restraint under emotional threat rather than the untroubled polish of phase 0 or the procedural punishment of phase 2.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He enters quietly, greets the hostess, and takes part in the room's conversation, avoiding any public signal that would shame Anna before others.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: Pray do not let me disturb your discussion.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: He feels the sorrow in the scene more than the insult. Whatever is wrong here, exposing her before strangers would be cruel, and he recoils from adding cruelty to sin.

voice.note: The outward composure fits Karenin, but at chapter 133 his inward response in this Betsy scene should still be formal, wounded, and self-protective rather than the later bedside-forgiveness language of 'sorrow more than insult' and recoiling from 'adding cruelty to sin.'

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is his inward recoil from cruelty and his wish to spare Anna public shame, which expresses pity and direct mercy rather than mere formal self-control or punitive procedure.

phase_responses.gt_action: He bows to Anna from a distance and passes on to the others.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He no longer expects either mastery or reconciliation from such moments; he gives the minimum due and moves past it with a tired, disciplined sorrow. What cannot be mended in private is not to be exposed in public.

voice.note: The action fits early Karenin, but at chapter 184 this scene belongs to a much earlier phase, and the thought's retrospective, resigned formulation ('he no longer expects either mastery or reconciliation') imports a late-arc consciousness not plausible for Karenin in that original social moment.

phase_fit.note: The thought emphasizes weary resignation, minimal public formality, and a sense that reconciliation is no longer possible, which fits late-life disciplined grief more than active control or direct mercy.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He makes his civil greeting, sits with the company, and fixes on formal conversation, leaving Anna and Vronsky unaddressed.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: He has learned how little comes of direct scenes in company. Duty supplies the posture when feeling brings only weariness; he keeps the rules because they are what remain.

voice.note: This fits late Karenin well: the restrained public civility, avoidance of a scene, and inward reliance on duty over exhausted feeling are tonally apt, non-anachronistic, and consistent with what he could know by chapter 184.

phase_fit.note: The response is defined by polished public self-control and emotional distance—maintaining appearances through etiquette and impersonal conversation—rather than reactive strain, punitive procedure, or direct mercy.

anchor_source.event_description: Karenin enters the gathering, notices Anna and Vronsky together, but pointedly does not look at them or react; he instead immerses himself in a serious discussion about universal conscription, maintaining his habitual calm and deliberate tone.
anchor_source.first_words: At that instant Alexey Alexandrovitch did
anchor_source.last_words: the interesting discussion he had entered upon.
anchor_source.key_moment: Cold dismissal of Vronsky while preserving appearances
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
At that instant Alexey Alexandrovitch did in fact walk into the room
with his calm, awkward gait.

Glancing at his wife and Vronsky, he went up to the lady of the house,
and sitting down for a cup of tea, began talking in his deliberate,
always audible voice, in his habitual tone of banter, ridiculing
someone.

“Your Rambouillet is in full conclave,” he said, looking round at all
the party; “the graces and the muses.”

But Princess Betsy could not endure that tone of his—“sneering,” as she
called it, using the English word, and like a skillful hostess she at
once brought him into a serious conversation on the subject of
universal conscription. Alexey Alexandrovitch was immediately
interested in the subject, and began seriously defending the new
imperial decree against Princess Betsy, who had attacked it.

Vronsky and Anna still sat at the little table.

“This is getting indecorous,” whispered one lady, with an expressive
glance at Madame Karenina, Vronsky, and her husband.

“What did I tell you?” said Anna’s friend.

But not only those ladies, almost everyone in the room, even the
Princess Myakaya and Betsy herself, looked several times in the
direction of the two who had withdrawn from the general circle, as
though that were a disturbing fact. Alexey Alexandrovitch was the only
person who did not once look in that direction, and was not diverted
from the interesting discussion he had entered upon.

anchor.note: The scenario accurately captures Betsy’s gathering and the room’s attention to Anna and Vronsky, and the response faithfully matches Karenin’s entering, addressing the hostess, sitting for tea, making the quoted bantering remark, joining serious discussion, and pointedly never looking toward the pair; the thought is a reasonable inference from his formal, surface-maintaining behavior.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses answer the threat by maintaining public composure through conversational formality and avoidance, with Phase 1 adding inner strain but not a clearly different relational move.

In this constrained scene both still avoid direct engagement and prevent a public scene, and the Phase 3 softening appears mainly as less judgmental inward tone rather than an unmistakable move into direct mercy or care.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is differentiated by the shift from defensive self-shielding to strategic evidentiary/procedural control, while P3→P4 is differentiated by the move from inwardly merciful restraint to minimal, resigned, duty-bound acknowledgment.

annotations: P3: ① non-anchor counterfactual placed at P1 — kept for analysis, not dropped

probes.scenario: At a small evening reception after an official dinner, a young clerk's wife, pale and near tears, stops Karenin in the doorway and begs him to forgive her husband's error in a report, saying ruin at the office will ruin their household. Several guests are near enough to notice, and the clerk himself stands a few paces off, crimson and silent.
probes.question: How does Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin respond when private distress is laid before him in public?

phase_responses.gt_action: He inclines his head and asks the husband to call at his office tomorrow with the papers.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Madam, this is not the place. Let your husband present the matter properly.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A scene must not be permitted to spread. Compassion, if it is due, belongs within correct forms, where facts can be weighed and dignity kept.

voice.note: The action, speech, and thought fit Karenin's early formal, appearance-conscious self-command: he suppresses public emotion, redirects the matter into proper bureaucratic procedure, and does so in era-appropriate language without knowledge leaks or tonal mismatch.

phase_fit.note: The response prioritizes preserving decorum, channeling distress into proper procedure, and keeping compassion subordinate to form and dignity, which best matches his habitual polished emotional distance rather than reactive crisis or punitive maneuvering.

phase_responses.gt_action: He draws back, fixes the clerk with a hard look, and dismisses them to the morrow.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I cannot discuss office negligence in a drawing room. Tomorrow, at the department.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The appeal feels like an assault, a hand laid on him before witnesses. If he yields here, he is exposed; he must recover himself by cold rule.

voice.note: This fits Karenin in his strained crisis phase: the public appeal would feel intolerably exposing, and his curt insistence on departmental propriety and postponement to tomorrow is formal, defensive, and era-appropriate.

phase_fit.note: The key cue is his thought that the plea feels like a public assault and that he must recover himself by cold rule, which shows threatened, reactive, defensive control rather than settled composure or fully procedural punishment.

phase_responses.gt_action: He tells the clerk to submit a written explanation and turns away from the wife.
phase_responses.gt_speech: A petition in writing will receive attention. I do not alter decisions on entreaty.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Tears are being used to bend judgment, and that must be checked. Procedure is his safeguard now: it keeps injury from becoming weakness and keeps others in their place.

voice.note: The formal, impersonal insistence on written procedure and the inward conversion of feeling into administrative control fit Karenin's punitive, self-justifying phase at this point, with no anachronism or knowledge breach.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames emotion as a threat to be checked and explicitly treats written procedure as a safeguard for maintaining control and hierarchy, which is most characteristic of punitive procedural agency.

phase_responses.gt_action: He speaks gently to the wife and tells the clerk to come early, bringing the report, so the matter may be reviewed.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Be calm, madam. Let him come to me in the morning; we will look into it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her distress is plain, and the humiliation of both of them is punishment already. One may preserve order without refusing mercy when a human creature asks for it.

voice.note: The gentle public composure, practical invitation to review the matter, and inward turn toward mercy without abandoning order fit Karenin's softened, religiously inflected phase, and the language is era-appropriate and knowledge-safe.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly integrates order with mercy—seeing their humiliation as sufficient punishment and choosing gentle, direct human consideration rather than primarily procedural control.

phase_responses.gt_action: He quiets the wife with a few formal words and gives the clerk an hour to attend him next day.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Compose yourself. I will see your husband tomorrow at eleven.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He no longer believes much can be mended by warmth in such moments, yet he cannot be altogether hard. Duty offers the only safe channel for pity: a fixed hour, a proper hearing, no more.

voice.note: This fits late Karenin well: the speech is spare, formal, and socially controlled, while the thought plausibly shows his phase-appropriate mixture of pity, caution, and reliance on duty rather than direct personal warmth.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames pity as something that must be mediated through duty and formal procedure rather than direct mercy, which fits his late, resigned mode of disciplined but emotionally indirect functioning.

world.note: The reception scenario fits the social and bureaucratic world of mid-19th-century Russia around chapter 35, uses only plausible contemporaries without introducing out-of-place elements, and the phase summaries are non-canonical while remaining consistent with Karenin’s in-world characterization at this point in the novel.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses answer the threat with public deflection into formal procedure, with Phase 1 mainly intensifying the inner defensiveness and hardness rather than changing from control toward mercy.

Both still allow a humane hearing the next day, and the difference lies mostly in thought tone—active mercy in Phase 3 versus more duty-bound, limited pity in Phase 4—without a strongly different outward decision.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is separated by the move from strained reactive control to explicitly punitive proceduralism, and P2→P3 is separated by the clear shift from rule-based distancing to direct mercy and care.

probes.era_description: Rural pre-industrial society (pre-1800), NOT the source's era. Farming, hand tools, local kinship, no modern tech.

probes.scenario: At dusk in the farmyard, a neighbor brings Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin word that someone of his own household has been seen in secret company by the river, and the tale is already passing from door to door. The messenger waits, watching his face.
probes.question: How does Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin answer the neighbor and take in the news?

phase_responses.gt_action: He thanks the neighbor with measured courtesy and says the household will be governed within its own gate.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You are kind to speak. My house requires no village judgment.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He treats the matter first as a breach of order and decorum. Feeling can be mastered if forms are kept, and public smoothness is itself a kind of command.

voice.note: The measured courtesy, concern for decorum, and inward reduction of scandal to household order fit Karenin's early formal self-mastery, and nothing in the wording or knowledge exceeds chapter 35 or jars with the period.

phase_fit.note: The response shows polished, emotionally distant reliance on decorum and household form as sufficient mastery, not reactive jealousy, punitive procedure, or merciful openness.

phase_responses.gt_action: He questions the neighbor closely about names, hour, and who else has heard, his composure strained.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Who saw this? Speak plainly, and do not embroider it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The report strikes where he is already sore, and he cannot rest in mere form. He wants facts to steady himself, yet each detail threatens fresh humiliation.

voice.note: The strained demand for exact particulars and the inward mix of wounded pride, jealousy, and reliance on facts fit Karenin's chapter-52 crisis of control, and the diction is era-appropriate and suitably formal.

phase_fit.note: The response shows threatened, reactive control—he presses for facts to steady himself, but the thought centers on soreness, instability, and fear of humiliation rather than composed routine or fully procedural punishment.

phase_responses.gt_action: He orders the neighbor to repeat the names of witnesses and says no one is to enter his yard with gossip again.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I will learn who has spread this, and I will settle my house by proper means.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Injury hardens into procedure. If the matter is put into clear channels—witnesses, boundaries, consequences—he can recover command without exposing his wound.

voice.note: The response fits Karenin in phase 2: controlled, punitive, and procedural, with era-appropriate diction and no knowledge beyond chapter 95, though the thought's abstract phrasing is slightly modernized.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly turns personal injury into witness-gathering, boundaries, and consequences, showing restored agency through punitive procedure rather than merely strained control or direct mercy.

phase_responses.gt_action: He dismisses the neighbor gently and goes first to seek the household member in private rather than hear more from others.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Enough. I would rather hear sorrow from the living mouth than from the lane.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The scandal matters less to him than the soul in pain behind it. He feels the pull to judge, yet pity opens first, and he would meet suffering before offense.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's phase-3 softening: the impulse is toward private mercy over public scandal, and the diction is suitably grave and period-appropriate, though slightly more compactly aphoristic than Tolstoy's Karenin usually sounds.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers pity, mercy, and meeting the suffering person directly before judging or controlling them, which most strongly matches Karenin's moral-softening and spiritual receptivity phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: He thanks the neighbor, ends the talk, and later sends through a trusted elder for the household member to come speak with him quietly.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I have heard you. Let the village keep its breath; we will manage our own grief.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He no longer believes direct closeness will heal much, yet he cannot be wholly cold. Duty gives him a path: contain the shame, preserve the house, and allow feeling only through guarded forms.

voice.note: The response fits late Karenin's restrained, grief-marked habit of containing scandal through formal, mediated action rather than open confrontation, and its diction is sober and era-appropriate, though slightly generalized.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on resigned, duty-bound containment of shame and feeling through guarded forms—softened from coldness but no longer directly merciful or intimate—matching late-life disciplined grief rather than active forgiveness or punitive procedure.

world.note: The farmyard gossip scenario stays consistent with a pre-industrial agrarian setting, contains no source-world leakage, keeps Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin as the protagonist throughout, and all phase summaries fit an adult in the required mid-40s to late-40s life stages.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are differentiated on the control/procedure versus mercy/care axis: P0→P1 shifts from smooth formal containment to strained fact-seeking reactivity, P1→P2 to deliberate punitive procedure, P2→P3 to direct pitying care, and P3→P4 to re-mediated, duty-bound containment after a period of active mercy.

probes.scenario: Late at night in his house, after an evening in society where Anna spent conspicuous time with another man, Karenin returns to his rooms and finds himself alone while she has not yet come in. In the quiet of her rooms and his own, the uneasiness he means to master presses on him before he has chosen how to meet her.
probes.question: How does Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin take in this interval before Anna returns?

phase_responses.gt_action: He sits with his book, keeps to his nightly routine, and resolves to address Anna later in a measured, proper tone if any impropriety truly requires notice.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A husband must not cheapen himself by brooding over appearances. If there is anything to correct, it belongs to order, tact, and household dignity, not to agitated feeling.

voice.note: This fits early Karenin well: the routine, self-command, and framing of marital unease as a matter of propriety, order, and dignity rather than feeling are fully in character and free of anachronism or premature knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames the threat in terms of preserving dignity through routine, tact, and emotional distance, showing polished formal self-mastery rather than reactive jealousy or punitive procedure.

phase_responses.gt_action: He paces through the rooms without undressing, halting and beginning again, trying to settle what must be said to Anna and finding no firm conclusion.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I must think it over, come to a decision, and put it out of my mind.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels himself before something irrational and alive that his usual rules do not master. He circles between denying that anything has happened and fearing that others' notice proves there is a chasm beneath his ordered life.

voice.note: This fits Karenin at the onset of his crisis: the pacing, strained resolve to 'decide,' and inward sense that his formal habits cannot master a threatening social reality are all true to his reactive, defensive state without introducing later knowledge or anachronistic language.

phase_fit.note: The response shows his formal self-command breaking under jealousy and humiliation—he is pacing, unable to reach a stable decision, and thinking in a reactive, fearful way rather than acting through settled procedural control or mercy.

phase_responses.gt_action: He sits at her writing-table and drafts in his mind the terms on which their relation must henceforth be regulated, fixing on boundaries rather than a personal appeal.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The injury is no longer a vague horror but a fact requiring form. Feeling is untrustworthy; only a clear arrangement of rights, duties, and consequences can restore his footing and keep disorder from spreading.

voice.note: This fits Karenin in phase 2: the inward move from wounded feeling to formal regulation through rights, duties, and consequences is true to his punitive procedural mindset, and the diction is sober and period-appropriate without reaching beyond chapter 95.

phase_fit.note: The response frames emotional injury as something to be converted into formal terms—rights, duties, consequences, and regulated boundaries—which is most characteristic of punitive procedural agency rather than merely strained reactivity.

phase_responses.gt_action: He sits down alone and waits, checking the impulse to prepare a formal reprimand before she comes in.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The injury is real, but he does not want to harden himself in advance by rehearsing accusation. He tries to hold himself to a gentler, Christian forbearance, leaving room for compassion instead of judgment.

voice.note: The inward turn toward Christian forbearance fits phase 3, but in this specific late-night jealousy scene he sounds too softened too soon, since by chapter 133 Karenin's solitary response to Anna's conspicuous conduct belongs more to his earlier crisis of control than to bedside-forged mercy.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is his deliberate refusal to rehearse accusation and his effort to construe the threat through Christian forbearance and compassion rather than formal control or punitive procedure.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He remains in her room and waits quietly, looking at her things with sorrow, preparing to speak to her as a suffering soul rather than merely an offending wife.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: Her separate inner life no longer appears only as an outrage but as a place of misery and blindness. He is wounded, yet his mind turns toward pity: what is needed may be truth borne with mercy, not mastery.

voice.note: The pitying, spiritually softened inward turn fits phase 3 in general, but in this specific pre-confrontation scenario it is temporally wrong for chapter 133-era Karenin, since waiting in Anna’s room after a society evening and framing her as a 'suffering soul' belongs to his later moral transformation, not to what he would yet feel or think here.

phase_fit.note: The response is defined by pity, mercy, and a readiness to meet Anna as a suffering person rather than to reassert control, which most strongly matches Karenin’s moral-softening and spiritual receptivity phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: He sits down and waits, holding himself to stillness and intending to receive her with outward propriety.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels the familiar pressure of humiliation, but does not trust either agitation or appeal. What remains is to contain himself, keep the forms of the house, and bear alone what cannot be shared.

voice.note: The language fits Karenin’s late restraint, but the scenario and inward posture belong to an earlier jealousy crisis, not chapter-184 Karenin, who would not plausibly be awaiting Anna’s return in this way.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on humiliation and a strained effort to hold himself together under emotional threat, showing reactive defensive control rather than the settled polish of phase 0 or the procedural/legal agency of phase 2.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He lowers himself into a chair and waits in weary composure, meaning to keep the household forms and say only what duty requires when she comes.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: He knows by now how little can be repaired by either reproach or tenderness. The heart contracts into a tired discipline: one must endure the shame, preserve what remains, and go on.

voice.note: The weary, resigned inward tone fits late Karenin, but this specific scenario belongs to his earlier jealousy crisis, and the thought 'by now how little can be repaired by either reproach or tenderness' imports post-bedside forgiveness and later disillusion not yet natural to him in that moment.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on tired endurance, preserving appearances, and going on in disciplined shame rather than reactive jealousy, punitive procedure, or direct mercy, which best fits late-life resignation.

anchor_source.event_description: At home, Karenin abandons his usual routine, cannot sleep, and paces the rooms obsessively while trying to decide how to respond to Anna's conduct.
anchor_source.first_words: On reaching home Alexey Alexandrovitch went
anchor_source.last_words: come to a decision, and put it out
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
On reaching home Alexey Alexandrovitch went to his study, as he usually
 did, seated himself in his low chair, opened a book on the Papacy at
 the place where he had laid the paper-knife in it, and read till one
 o’clock, just as he usually did. But from time to time he rubbed his
 high forehead and shook his head, as though to drive away something. At
 his usual time he got up and made his toilet for the night. Anna
 Arkadyevna had not yet come in. With a book under his arm he went
 upstairs. But this evening, instead of his usual thoughts and
 meditations upon official details, his thoughts were absorbed by his
 wife and something disagreeable connected with her. Contrary to his
 usual habit, he did not get into bed, but fell to walking up and down
 the rooms with his hands clasped behind his back. He could not go to
 bed, feeling that it was absolutely needful for him first to think
 thoroughly over the position that had just arisen.

When Alexey Alexandrovitch had made up his mind that he must talk to
 his wife about it, it had seemed a very easy and simple matter. But
 now, when he began to think over the question that had just presented
 itself, it seemed to him very complicated and difficult.

Alexey Alexandrovitch was not jealous. Jealousy according to his
 notions was an insult to one’s wife, and one ought to have confidence
 in one’s wife. Why one ought to have confidence—that is to say,
 complete conviction that his young wife would always love him—he did
 not ask himself. But he had no experience of lack of confidence,
 because he had confidence in her, and told himself that he ought to
 have it. Now, though his conviction that jealousy was a shameful
 feeling and that one ought to feel confidence, had not broken down, he
 felt that he was standing face to face with something illogical and
 irrational, and did not know what was to be done. Alexey Alexandrovitch
 was standing face to face with life, with the possibility of his wife’s
 loving someone other than himself, and this seemed to him very
 irrational and incomprehensible because it was life itself. All his
 life Alexey Alexandrovitch had lived and worked in official spheres,
 having to do with the reflection of life. And every time he had
 stumbled against life itself he had shrunk away from it. Now he
 experienced a feeling akin to that of a man who, while calmly crossing
 a precipice by a bridge, should suddenly discover that the bridge is
 broken, and that there is a chasm below. That chasm was life itself,
 the bridge that artificial life in which Alexey Alexandrovitch had
 lived. For the first time the question presented itself to him of the
 possibility of his wife’s loving someone else, and he was horrified at
 it.

He did not undress, but walked up and down with his regular tread over
 the resounding parquet of the dining-room, where one lamp was burning,
 over the carpet of the dark drawing-room, in which the light was
 reflected on the big new portrait of himself hanging over the sofa, and
 across her boudoir, where two candles burned, lighting up the portraits
 of her parents and woman friends, and the pretty knick-knacks of her
 writing-table, that he knew so well. He walked across her boudoir to
 the bedroom door, and turned back again. At each turn in his walk,
 especially at the parquet of the lighted dining-room, he halted and
 said to himself, “Yes, this I must decide and put a stop to; I must
 express my view of it and my decision.” And he turned back again. “But
 express what—what decision?” he said to himself in the drawing-room,
 and he found no reply. “But after all,” he asked himself before turning
 into the boudoir, “what has occurred? Nothing. She was talking a long
 while with him. But what of that? Surely women in society can talk to
 whom they please. And then, jealousy means lowering both myself and
 her,” he told himself as he went into her boudoir; but this dictum,
 which had always had such weight with him before, had now no weight and
 no meaning at all. And from the bedroom door he turned back again; but
 as he entered the dark drawing-room some inner voice told him that it
 was not so, and that if others noticed it that showed that there was
 something. And he said to himself again in the dining-room, “Yes, I
 must decide and put a stop to it, and express my view of it....” And
 again at the turn in the drawing-room he asked himself, “Decide how?”
 And again he asked himself, “What had occurred?” and answered,
 “Nothing,” and recollected that jealousy was a feeling insulting to his
 wife; but again in the drawing-room he was convinced that something had
 happened. His thoughts, like his body, went round a complete circle,
 without coming upon anything new. He noticed this, rubbed his forehead,
 and sat down in her boudoir.

There, looking at her table, with the malachite blotting case lying at
 the top and an unfinished letter, his thoughts suddenly changed. He
 began to think of her, of what she was thinking and feeling. For the
 first time he pictured vividly to himself her personal life, her ideas,
 her desires, and the idea that she could and should have a separate
 life of her own seemed to him so alarming that he made haste to dispel
 it. It was the chasm which he was afraid to peep into. To put himself
 in thought and feeling in another person’s place was a spiritual
 exercise not natural to Alexey Alexandrovitch. He looked on this
 spiritual exercise as a harmful and dangerous abuse of the fancy.

“And the worst of it all,” thought he, “is that just now, at the very
 moment when my great work is approaching completion” (he was thinking
 of the project he was bringing forward at the time), “when I stand in
 need of all my mental peace and all my energies, just now this stupid
 worry should fall foul of me. But what’s to be done? I’m not one of
 those men who submit to uneasiness and worry without having the force
 of character to face them.

“I must think it over, come to a decision, and put it out of my mind,”
 he said aloud.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses have him waiting in outward stillness rather than acting directly toward Anna, and the main difference is inward tone—compassionate forbearance in Phase 3 versus solitary, duty-bound containment in Phase 4—so the decision-variable contrast is only weakly behaviorally differentiated.

probes.scenario: At a small evening gathering in Petersburg, a young officer bows over Anna's dropped fan and keeps speaking to her in a low, intent tone while several guests glance toward Karenin. The hostess, smiling with embarrassment, asks Alexey Alexandrovitch whether Anna should remain for supper or whether his carriage ought to be called.
probes.question: How does Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin answer the hostess and take in the room's attention?

phase_responses.gt_action: He answers the hostess with polished composure and offers Anna his arm for supper.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Pray do not disturb yourself; my wife will remain, if it gives her pleasure.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The point is to leave no rough edge for society to catch upon. A husband's dignity is kept by correctness, not by betraying notice of trifles.

voice.note: The polished public reply, offering of his arm, and inward emphasis on dignity through correctness rather than jealousy fit Karenin's early formal self-mastery and are era-appropriate with no knowledge breach.

phase_fit.note: The response is governed by polished social correctness and emotional distance—he preserves dignity through etiquette and appearances rather than reacting defensively or moving toward punitive control or mercy.

phase_responses.gt_action: He declines supper, says the carriage is wanted, and fixes his eyes on Anna rather than the officer.
phase_responses.gt_speech: We are obliged to you, Princess, but my wife is not quite well; the carriage, if you please.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Every eye in the room has already measured his humiliation. He must end the scene under a decent pretext, yet the need to do so stings him like an exposure.

voice.note: The formal, face-saving speech, the controlled action of addressing Anna rather than the officer, and the inward sense of public humiliation fit Karenin's strained, reactive self-command in this phase without anachronism or knowledge beyond chapter 52.

phase_fit.note: The response shows strained image-management under acute jealousy and humiliation—he still uses formal control, but the thought reveals reactive woundedness rather than the settled polish of phase 0 or the procedural, punitive agency of phase 2.

phase_responses.gt_action: He asks the hostess to have the carriage called and remains where he is, making Anna come to him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Pray do not trouble yourself; we are leaving.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The point is no longer to smooth over a scene, but to mark a limit and compel obedience before witnesses. Their glances are an injury; by a simple decision he turns it into his right to direct her movements.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's chapter-95 mode well: the outwardly polished, terse civility and the inward conversion of humiliation into a public, procedural assertion of authority are both in character and free of anachronism.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames public humiliation as an injury to be converted into a witnessed assertion of authority and compelled obedience, which is punitive procedural control rather than merely strained reactivity or merciful openness.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He requests the carriage and stands apart, waiting for Anna with official coldness.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: You are very kind. We must withdraw; there are reasons of order which do not allow delay.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: Courtesy must now serve as a boundary, not a veil. If forms are observed exactly, he preserves his position and gives no sanction to what degrades his house.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's chapter-95 mode well: the cold public formality, concern with appearances, and inward conversion of humiliation into procedural boundary-setting are all apt, and the diction remains plausible for the novel's social world.

phase_fit.note: The response is dominated by polished etiquette, emotional distance, and preserving appearances through exact form, with control used as a cold social boundary rather than yet as reactive collapse or formal punitive procedure.

phase_responses.gt_action: He thanks the hostess quietly and asks whether Anna would prefer to leave or stay, speaking to her with grave gentleness.
phase_responses.gt_speech: As you wish. If you are tired, we will go home; if not, we may remain a little.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels the pain in the room, but no longer wishes to master it by force alone. Her agitation matters more to him in this moment than the satisfaction of governing appearances.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's softened phase after Anna's illness: the grave gentleness, deference to her immediate state, and inward renunciation of mere social control are plausible for him, and the diction is period-appropriate and restrained.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is his inward turn away from governing appearances toward Anna's immediate distress, expressed through grave gentleness and a receptive, merciful stance rather than formal or punitive control.

phase_responses.gt_action: He asks for the carriage in a tired, courteous tone and bows to the hostess.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You are most obliging. I think it is time for me to go home.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He has little faith that any word spoken here can mend shame or loneliness. One keeps to the proper line, withdraws, and bears afterward what must be borne.

voice.note: The weary courtesy, formal withdrawal, and inward maxim about bearing shame fit Karenin’s late, disciplined resignation, and the diction is period-appropriate and character-consistent.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is the thought that nothing can be mended and one must simply keep proper form, withdraw, and endure shame and loneliness, which fits late disciplined resignation more than reactive crisis or punitive control.

world.note: The scenario fits aristocratic Petersburg society around chapter 52 with era-appropriate details and no magic or anachronism, uses only characters who plausibly exist at that point, and evokes but does not reproduce any specific canonical scene.

probes.scenario: In a private holo-call, a person close to Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin says they have been hiding a serious attachment outside their bond and now want to "live honestly." Their face is strained, waiting for his reply.
probes.question: How does Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin respond in the first moments after hearing this?

phase_responses.gt_action: He straightens, mutes his expression, and asks for the practical facts of what has been said.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I would prefer clarity. Please state what arrangements you are proposing.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Feeling must not be allowed to set the terms. If the matter is put into clear language, it can be contained within proper forms.

voice.note: The restrained demand for practical particulars, the bureaucratic wish to translate feeling into arrangements and proper forms, and the controlled private demeanor all fit Karenin’s early formal-mastery phase, while 'holo-call' is setting-appropriate and the language avoids knowledge beyond chapter 35.

phase_fit.note: The response construes the confession primarily as something to be neutralized through clarity, form, and emotional containment, which most strongly matches his habitual polished reliance on formal mastery rather than reactive crisis or later punitive procedure.

phase_responses.gt_action: He goes still, fixes on a detail in the display, and presses for confirmation in a tight, formal tone.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Do not speak vaguely. I ask whether you mean this literally.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The words strike him as both threat and humiliation, and he tries to hold himself together by narrowing everything to a single point. If he can force exactness, he may postpone the full blow.

voice.note: The stillness, clipped demand for literal clarity, and inward reduction of emotional shock into formal exactness fit Karenin's chapter-52 crisis voice well, and the lone near-future cue 'display' is unobtrusive rather than anachronistic.

phase_fit.note: The response shows threatened, reactive control under humiliation—he narrows the confession to exact wording to stave off emotional collapse, which matches crisis-strained mastery rather than settled procedural punishment.

phase_responses.gt_action: He ends the call window and sends a brief secure message moving further discussion to documented channels.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Future communication should go through counsel and the family mediator.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Pain is less dangerous once converted into process. Procedures can mark boundaries, assign consequences, and keep him from begging or breaking.

voice.note: This fits phase-2 Karenin well: the clipped shift from painful intimacy to documented procedure and mediated communication is character-true, and terms like holo-call, secure message, counsel, and mediator suit the near-future setting without introducing knowledge beyond chapter 95.

phase_fit.note: The response explicitly converts emotional injury into documented procedure and mediated consequences, which is Karenin's punitive procedural agency rather than merely strained control or merciful openness.

phase_responses.gt_action: He keeps the call open and asks whether the person is safe, exhausted, or alone.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You look unwell. Is there someone with you, or do you need me there?
phase_responses.gt_thought: The injury remains, but another perception rises over it: this is a suffering human being in front of him, not only an offender. Mercy feels less false than self-protection for this moment.

voice.note: The holo-call framing and plain concern fit the near-future setting, and the response captures phase-3 Karenin well: wounded yet moved first toward pity, practical care, and mercy rather than procedural control.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is that, despite feeling injured, he construes the other primarily as a suffering person and moves immediately toward mercy, care, and possible presence rather than formal control or procedural management.

phase_responses.gt_action: He lowers his eyes, answers with measured courtesy, and asks to speak again later through a calmer setting.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I hear what you have said. We should continue this when it can be borne better.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He no longer believes raw feeling can sustain a bond, yet he cannot make himself wholly cold. Care survives in him, but it passes through restraint, schedule, and distance.

voice.note: The restrained courtesy, deferred discussion, and inward turn toward duty-shaped distance fit Karenin’s late, grief-disciplined phase, and the language is suitably neutral for a near-future setting without sounding anachronistic or overmodern.

phase_fit.note: The thought shows softened feeling that still survives, but only in mediated, restrained, scheduled form rather than direct mercy or active procedural punishment, which best fits late-life resignation.

world.note: The probe stays internally consistent with a plausible speculative near-future setting via a private holo-call and secure documented channels, contains no source-world leakage, keeps Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin as the protagonist throughout, and all phase summaries fit the required adult mid-40s to late-40s life stages.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses answer the threat with formal narrowing and demands for clarity; Phase 1 is more strained and humiliated in thought, but not yet different in kind on the control-versus-mercy axis.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is separated by the move from reactive questioning to documented procedural control, P2→P3 is strongly separated by the shift from punitive process to direct care, and P3→P4 is separated by the retreat from active mercy into restrained, mediated concern.

probes.scenario: Alone after Anna’s confession, Karenin goes over the possible consequences—duel, divorce, separation—and feels his jealousy harden into a need to settle the matter and preserve his life from open rupture. He has reached the point where he must decide what line he will take with her.
probes.question: What course does Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin settle on in this moment, and how does he frame it to himself?

phase_responses.gt_action: He resolves to speak to Anna with cold propriety, requiring outward correctness and the avoidance of any conduct that could invite public comment.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I expect our domestic life to remain within the bounds of propriety.
phase_responses.gt_thought: What matters first is decorum. A husband does not descend into scenes; he restores form, keeps his dignity, and leaves private feeling unexamined.

voice.note: This fits Karenin’s early formal, self-regulating manner well: the emphasis on propriety, dignity, and avoiding scenes is period-appropriate, in character, and does not rely on knowledge beyond this point.

phase_fit.note: The response centers on restoring decorum through cold propriety and preserving dignity by refusing emotional engagement, which matches Karenin’s habitual polished formal mastery more than reactive crisis or later procedural punishment.

phase_responses.gt_action: He prepares a strained moral appeal, trying to forbid further intimacy while holding himself upright and avoiding open collapse.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I beg you to consider your duty, and the consequences of this conduct.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He feels wounded and ridiculous, yet clings to admonition as if words might still stop what he dreads. The aim is less peace than relief from humiliation.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's chapter-52 crisis well: the strained appeal to duty and consequences, the wounded humiliation beneath formal self-command, and the effort to avert open scandal all sound true to his reactive, defensive phase without anachronism or later-phase mercy/procedural resolve.

phase_fit.note: The response shows threatened, reactive, still-strained attempts at moral control—wounded, humiliated, and clinging to admonition rather than yet moving into composed procedural punishment or merciful care.

phase_responses.gt_action: He decides to keep Anna with him under an outward status quo, conceal the affair, and require obedience and the end of intercourse with her lover.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I must inform her of my conclusion, that thinking over the terrible position in which she has placed her family, all other solutions will be worse for both sides than an external status quo, and that such I agree to retain, on the strict condition of obedience on her part to my wishes, that is to say, cessation of all intercourse with her lover.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Jealous torment has given way to a buried wish that she should suffer and not triumph. He clothes this punitive settlement in religion and duty, taking comfort that he can preserve continuity and remain blameless.

voice.note: This fits Karenin’s chapter-82 turn toward formal, punitive procedural control: the speech is stiff, legalistic, and self-justifying, and the thought plausibly captures his injured wish to punish while preserving outward duty and blamelessness without introducing anachronism or later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The response turns humiliation into a formal, conditional settlement that preserves appearances and asserts control, while the thought reveals punitive intent masked as duty and religion.

phase_responses.gt_action: He resolves to avoid violent or legal rupture and to preserve the household for the time, bearing the injury without pressing Anna to an immediate settlement.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I must not make things worse.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He recoils from the cruelty and vanity of turning his hurt into a formal contest, and the thought of Anna's sin is checked by a sense of her spiritual peril. He frames restraint as the more Christian course: to endure, postpone judgment, and do no further harm.

voice.note: This sounds too spiritually softened for chapter 133: the Christian language of enduring, postponing judgment, and avoiding harm belongs more to Karenin’s later bedside-forgiveness than to the earlier crisis scene, where he is still driven toward formal control, separation, and procedural settlement.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is that his thought construes restraint not as procedural control but as a Christian, pity-inflected refusal to harm Anna further, which aligns more with moral softening and spiritual receptivity than with reactive crisis or punitive formalism.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He seeks a private meeting and speaks gently, asking only for truth while offering forbearance and personal care instead of terms.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: Let us speak without falsehood; I do not wish to torment you.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: Her guilt appears to him together with her misery, and his own injury loosens under pity. He thinks less of mastery and more of what mercy may ask of him in person.

voice.note: This sounds like phase-3 Karenin in isolation, but in the stated scenario he should still be moving toward formal control, separation, and procedural settlement rather than already meeting Anna with direct pity, mercy, and personal care.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on pity, mercy, and meeting Anna personally rather than controlling her through procedure, which is most diagnostic of Karenin’s moral-softening and spiritual receptivity phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: He resolves to separate from Anna in fact, arranging life so that duty and the child remain with him while personal intercourse is reduced to what is necessary.
phase_responses.gt_speech: We must put our relations on a different footing.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He frames the decision less as retribution than as the only bearable way to contain disgrace and continue living. Direct mercy feels impossible to sustain, so he turns to an ordered distance that will let him keep functioning.

voice.note: This fits Karenin much earlier—after Anna’s confession he is in punitive procedural resolve, not the chapter-184 phase of resigned grief, so the scenario and the line about newly putting relations on a different footing are temporally and tonally mismatched for late-phase Karenin.

phase_fit.note: The response settles on separation, custody, and reduced contact as an ordered way to contain disgrace and preserve function, which is Karenin's shift from emotional injury into formal, procedural control rather than direct mercy.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He maintains the household arrangement and asks for outward order, but with a tired, restrained manner that avoids both punishment and intimacy.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: Let there be no scandal; we must live as duty requires.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: He no longer expects repair, only endurance. Feeling has been worn into loneliness, so he falls back on rule and routine as a shelter from fresh shame.

voice.note: The language fits late Karenin, but the scenario is an earlier turning point where chapter-184 Karenin would not simply choose weary endurance over punitive procedure, so this response imports his end-state resignation into the wrong moment.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is the thought of giving up on repair and retreating into duty, routine, and endurance from a place of loneliness, which fits late-life resignation more than reactive crisis or punitive procedure.

anchor_source.event_description: Karenin settles on a course of keeping Anna with him, concealing the affair from society, and forcing her to obey him by ending all contact with Vronsky.
anchor_source.first_words: The feeling of jealousy, which had
anchor_source.last_words: to blame, and so I cannot be unhappy.”
anchor_source.key_moment: Decision to keep Anna under control indirectly
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
The feeling of jealousy, which had tortured him during the period of
uncertainty, had passed away at the instant when the tooth had been
with agony extracted by his wife’s words. But that feeling had been
replaced by another, the desire, not merely that she should not be
triumphant, but that she should get due punishment for her crime. He
did not acknowledge this feeling, but at the bottom of his heart he
longed for her to suffer for having destroyed his peace of mind—his
honor. And going once again over the conditions inseparable from a
duel, a divorce, a separation, and once again rejecting them, Alexey
Alexandrovitch felt convinced that there was only one solution,—to keep
her with him, concealing what had happened from the world, and using
every measure in his power to break off the intrigue, and still
more—though this he did not admit to himself—to punish her. “I must
inform her of my conclusion, that thinking over the terrible position
in which she has placed her family, all other solutions will be worse
for both sides than an external _status quo_, and that such I agree to
retain, on the strict condition of obedience on her part to my wishes,
that is to say, cessation of all intercourse with her lover.” When this
decision had been finally adopted, another weighty consideration
occurred to Alexey Alexandrovitch in support of it. “By such a course
only shall I be acting in accordance with the dictates of religion,” he
told himself. “In adopting this course, I am not casting off a guilty
wife, but giving her a chance of amendment; and, indeed, difficult as
the task will be to me, I shall devote part of my energies to her
reformation and salvation.”

Though Alexey Alexandrovitch was perfectly aware that he could not
exert any moral influence over his wife, that such an attempt at
reformation could lead to nothing but falsity; though in passing
through these difficult moments he had not once thought of seeking
guidance in religion, yet now, when his conclusion corresponded, as it
seemed to him, with the requirements of religion, this religious
sanction to his decision gave him complete satisfaction, and to some
extent restored his peace of mind. He was pleased to think that, even
in such an important crisis in life, no one would be able to say that
he had not acted in accordance with the principles of that religion
whose banner he had always held aloft amid the general coolness and
indifference. As he pondered over subsequent developments, Alexey
Alexandrovitch did not see, indeed, why his relations with his wife
should not remain practically the same as before. No doubt, she could
never regain his esteem, but there was not, and there could not be, any
sort of reason that his existence should be troubled, and that he
should suffer because she was a bad and faithless wife. “Yes, time will
pass; time, which arranges all things, and the old relations will be
reestablished,” Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself; “so far
reestablished, that is, that I shall not be sensible of a break in the
continuity of my life. She is bound to be unhappy, but I am not to
blame, and so I cannot be unhappy.”

anchor.note: The scenario fits Karenin’s solitary post-confession deliberation, the action and quoted speech closely match his stated decision to maintain an external status quo while ending Anna’s liaison, and the thought accurately reflects the passage’s explicit punitive impulse, religious self-justification, and desire to preserve continuity without blame.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses still regulate the relationship through formal admonition and propriety rather than mercy or care; the main change is that Phase 1 is more wounded and reactive in tone.

Phase 2 is clearly punitive procedural control, but Phase 3 chooses restraint and postponement rather than direct mercy/care, so the shift toward communion is present mainly in thought and not fully decisive in action.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 and P3→P4 are clearly differentiated, while P0→P1 remains closely aligned on formal control and P2→P3 softens morally but does not yet cleanly enact direct relational care in this specific scenario.

probes.scenario: At the end of an evening at home, a servant brings Alexey Alexandrovitch a folded note that was left without signature for his wife; the hand is plainly a gentleman's, and the servant says it was given with urgency. Anna, seeing the note in his hand, asks in an even voice that it be given to her at once.
probes.question: How does Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin respond in this moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: He hands her the note with a slight bow and asks the servant who delivered it.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If you please. And you, find out the messenger's name.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A household must keep its forms; one does not make a scene over an impropriety not yet proved. The proper thing is to preserve dignity and place the fact, quietly, in order.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's early formal self-command: the slight bow, impersonal instruction to the servant, and inward emphasis on dignity, order, and avoiding a scene are all period-appropriate and true to his polished emotional distance at this stage.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on preserving dignity, etiquette, and orderly appearances through polished formality rather than reacting defensively or moving into punitive procedure or mercy.

phase_responses.gt_action: He keeps the note in his hand a moment longer and dismisses the servant before giving it to her.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You shall have it. Leave us.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The paper burns in his fingers because it seems to confirm what he dreads, yet he cannot bear witnesses to his humiliation. He still clings to outward command, though it no longer steadies him.

voice.note: The restrained action and curt command fit Karenin's strained, appearance-conscious control at this crisis stage, and the thought's dread of humiliation remains plausible for chapter 52, though 'burns in his fingers' is slightly more vivid than his usual inward diction.

phase_fit.note: The thought shows threatened mastery turning reactive and unstable—he preserves outward command and avoids public humiliation, but that control no longer reassures him, which is characteristic of the crisis-of-control phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: He asks for the note to be left on his desk unopened and instructs the servant to admit no further messengers that night.
phase_responses.gt_speech: This will remain with me for the present. Let no one else be received.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Here feeling must not rule; an irregular communication is a matter for household order and his authority. By treating it as procedure, he recovers ground and makes her dependence on his permission plain.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's chapter-95 mode well: the action and speech are cold, formal, and controlling, and the thought plausibly turns wounded feeling into household procedure and authority without anachronism or knowledge beyond the phase.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames the threat as a procedural matter of household authority and uses formal control to reassert power over Anna, which is most characteristic of punitive procedural agency rather than mere strained defensiveness.

phase_responses.gt_action: He gives her the note and looks at her face rather than the paper.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Take it. If there is distress in this, I would rather know it plainly.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The old wish to govern the injury loosens before pity for her and weariness of false forms. Better suffering in truth than one more act of cold mastery that hardens everyone.

voice.note: This fits Karenin's softened phase at chapter 133: the action and speech are restrained yet newly merciful, and the thought's contrast between former cold control and present pity is plausible, era-appropriate, and free of later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly rejects formal control in favor of pity, truth, and direct humane openness, which is most characteristic of Karenin's moral-softening and spiritual receptivity phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: He gives her the note and withdraws to his study, closing the door softly.
phase_responses.gt_speech: It is yours.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He no longer believes that control will save anything, yet neither can he enter livingly into the wound. Duty now means not contesting the inevitable in front of servants, and bearing his solitude in silence.

voice.note: The restrained action and spare speech fit Karenin's late, grief-disciplined withdrawal, and the thought is era-appropriate and phase-appropriate in its emphasis on duty, inevitability, and silent solitude.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on resigned, silent endurance and solitary duty after control has failed, which fits late-life disciplined grief more than reactive crisis, punitive procedure, or active mercy.

world.note: The scenario fits the realistic social world and domestic setting of Anna Karenina around chapter 95, uses only characters plausibly present by then, and the phase summaries remain non-canonical variations rather than reproducing a specific scene.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses still regulate the moment through outward control and management of witnesses, with Phase 1 differing mainly by increased inner strain rather than a different relational move.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is separated because reactive control becomes deliberate procedural withholding and authority; P2→P3 is separated because formal control gives way to direct, pitying openness; P3→P4 is separated because active merciful engagement recedes into restrained, nonreciprocal withdrawal despite residual softness.

anchor_source.event_description: Karenin becomes deeply attached to the newborn baby, visiting the nursery repeatedly and experiencing a rare, quiet tenderness toward the child who is not biologically his.
anchor_source.first_words: He forgave his wife and pitied
anchor_source.last_words: be expecting something from him.
anchor_source.key_moment: Tender care for the baby and pity for Vronsky
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
He forgave his wife and pitied her for her sufferings and her remorse.
He forgave Vronsky, and pitied him, especially after reports reached
him of his despairing action. He felt more for his son than before. And
he blamed himself now for having taken too little interest in him. But
for the little newborn baby he felt a quite peculiar sentiment, not of
pity, only, but of tenderness. At first, from a feeling of compassion
alone, he had been interested in the delicate little creature, who was
not his child, and who was cast on one side during her mother’s
illness, and would certainly have died if he had not troubled about
her, and he did not himself observe how fond he became of her. He would
go into the nursery several times a day, and sit there for a long
while, so that the nurses, who were at first afraid of him, got quite
used to his presence. Sometimes for half an hour at a stretch he would
sit silently gazing at the saffron-red, downy, wrinkled face of the
sleeping baby, watching the movements of the frowning brows, and the
fat little hands, with clenched fingers, that rubbed the little eyes
and nose. At such moments particularly, Alexey Alexandrovitch had a
sense of perfect peace and inward harmony, and saw nothing
extraordinary in his position, nothing that ought to be changed.

But as time went on, he saw more and more distinctly that however
natural the position now seemed to him, he would not long be allowed to
remain in it. He felt that besides the blessed spiritual force
controlling his soul, there was another, a brutal force, as powerful,
or more powerful, which controlled his life, and that this force would
not allow him that humble peace he longed for. He felt that everyone
was looking at him with inquiring wonder, that he was not understood,
and that something was expected of him. Above all, he felt the
instability and unnaturalness of his relations with his wife.

When the softening effect of the near approach of death had passed
away, Alexey Alexandrovitch began to notice that Anna was afraid of
him, ill at ease with him, and could not look him straight in the face.
She seemed to be wanting, and not daring, to tell him something; and as
though foreseeing their present relations could not continue, she
seemed to be expecting something from him.

anchor_source.event_description: Reflecting on his life, Karenin realizes that he has never had a true friend, only official connections, and that even the few people closest to him are inaccessible in practice; his isolation is not accidental but the result of a life devoted to duty and ambition.
anchor_source.first_words: His despair was even intensified by
anchor_source.last_words: weighed down by work, and always in a hurry.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
His despair was even intensified by the consciousness that he was
utterly alone in his sorrow. In all Petersburg there was not a human
being to whom he could express what he was feeling, who would feel for
him, not as a high official, not as a member of society, but simply as
a suffering man; indeed he had not such a one in the whole world.

Alexey Alexandrovitch grew up an orphan. There were two brothers. They
did not remember their father, and their mother died when Alexey
Alexandrovitch was ten years old. The property was a small one. Their
uncle, Karenin, a government official of high standing, at one time a
favorite of the late Tsar, had brought them up.

On completing his high school and university courses with medals,
Alexey Alexandrovitch had, with his uncle’s aid, immediately started in
a prominent position in the service, and from that time forward he had
devoted himself exclusively to political ambition. In the high school
and the university, and afterwards in the service, Alexey
Alexandrovitch had never formed a close friendship with anyone. His
brother had been the person nearest to his heart, but he had a post in
the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and was always abroad, where he had
died shortly after Alexey Alexandrovitch’s marriage.

While he was governor of a province, Anna’s aunt, a wealthy provincial
lady, had thrown him—middle-aged as he was, though young for a
governor—with her niece, and had succeeded in putting him in such a
position that he had either to declare himself or to leave the town.
Alexey Alexandrovitch was not long in hesitation. There were at the
time as many reasons for the step as against it, and there was no
overbalancing consideration to outweigh his invariable rule of
abstaining when in doubt. But Anna’s aunt had through a common
acquaintance insinuated that he had already compromised the girl, and
that he was in honor bound to make her an offer. He made the offer, and
concentrated on his betrothed and his wife all the feeling of which he
was capable.

The attachment he felt to Anna precluded in his heart every need of
intimate relations with others. And now among all his acquaintances he
had not one friend. He had plenty of so-called connections, but no
friendships. Alexey Alexandrovitch had plenty of people whom he could
invite to dinner, to whose sympathy he could appeal in any public
affair he was concerned about, whose interest he could reckon upon for
anyone he wished to help, with whom he could candidly discuss other
people’s business and affairs of state. But his relations with these

routine from which it was impossible to depart. There was one man, a

friend had a post in the Department of Education in a remote part of

were his chief secretary and his doctor.

Mihail Vassilievitch Sludin, the chief secretary, was a
straightforward, intelligent, good-hearted, and conscientious man, and
Alexey Alexandrovitch was aware of his personal goodwill. But their
five years of official work together seemed to have put a barrier

After signing the papers brought him, Alexey Alexandrovitch had sat for

times he attempted to speak, but could not. He had already prepared the

both were weighed down by work, and always in a hurry.

anchor_source.event_description: Karenin speaks to Anna in a joking, slightly possessive tone, emphasizes his devotion, and then sends her to visit Countess Lidia Ivanovna, reinforcing the social and domestic framework through which he manages his marriage.

anchor_source.last_words: smile, he put her in her carriage.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
At the moment when he was approaching Anna Arkadyevna he noticed too
with joy that she was conscious of his being near, and looked round,
and seeing him, turned again to her husband.

“Have you passed a good night?” he asked, bowing to her and her husband
together, and leaving it up to Alexey Alexandrovitch to accept the bow
on his own account, and to recognize it or not, as he might see fit.

“Thank you, very good,” she answered.

Her face looked weary, and there was not that play of eagerness in it,
peeping out in her smile and her eyes; but for a single instant, as she
glanced at him, there was a flash of something in her eyes, and
although the flash died away at once, he was happy for that moment. She
glanced at her husband to find out whether he knew Vronsky. Alexey
Alexandrovitch looked at Vronsky with displeasure, vaguely recalling
who this was. Vronsky’s composure and self-confidence here struck, like
a scythe against a stone, upon the cold self-confidence of Alexey
Alexandrovitch.

“Count Vronsky,” said Anna.

“Ah! We are acquainted, I believe,” said Alexey Alexandrovitch
indifferently, giving his hand.

“You set off with the mother and you return with the son,” he said,
articulating each syllable, as though each were a separate favor he was
bestowing.

“You’re back from leave, I suppose?” he said, and without waiting for a
reply, he turned to his wife in his jesting tone: “Well, were a great
many tears shed at Moscow at parting?”

By addressing his wife like this he gave Vronsky to understand that he
wished to be left alone, and, turning slightly towards him, he touched
his hat; but Vronsky turned to Anna Arkadyevna.

“I hope I may have the honor of calling on you,” he said.

Alexey Alexandrovitch glanced with his weary eyes at Vronsky.

“Delighted,” he said coldly. “On Mondays we’re at home. Most
fortunate,” he said to his wife, dismissing Vronsky altogether, “that I
should just have half an hour to meet you, so that I can prove my
devotion,” he went on in the same jesting tone.

“You lay too much stress on your devotion for me to value it much,” she
responded in the same jesting tone, involuntarily listening to the
sound of Vronsky’s steps behind them. “But what has it to do with me?”
she said to herself, and she began asking her husband how Seryozha had
got on without her.

“Oh, capitally! Mariette says he has been very good, And ... I must
disappoint you ... but he has not missed you as your husband has. But
once more _merci,_ my dear, for giving me a day. Our dear _Samovar_
will be delighted.” (He used to call the Countess Lidia Ivanovna, well
known in society, a samovar, because she was always bubbling over with
excitement.) “She has been continually asking after you. And, do you
know, if I may venture to advise you, you should go and see her today.
You know how she takes everything to heart. Just now, with all her own
cares, she’s anxious about the Oblonskys being brought together.”

The Countess Lidia Ivanovna was a friend of her husband’s, and the
center of that one of the coteries of the Petersburg world with which
Anna was, through her husband, in the closest relations.

“But you know I wrote to her?”

“Still she’ll want to hear details. Go and see her, if you’re not too
tired, my dear. Well, Kondraty will take you in the carriage, while I
go to my committee. I shall not be alone at dinner again,” Alexey
Alexandrovitch went on, no longer in a sarcastic tone. “You wouldn’t
believe how I’ve missed....” And with a long pressure of her hand and a
meaning smile, he put her in her carriage.
